f5f9354f9147: Health disparities in rural Guatemala and the impact of Dr. Pelico’s clinic
17f9cb569717: Rural Guatemala faces some of the most severe health disparities in Central America, driven by geographic isolation, linguistic exclusion, chronic underfunding, and the near‑total absence of Indigenous‑speaking clinicians. This report brings together available public health data with on‑the‑ground findings from Aldea Pitzal, where Dr. Pelico is delivering a model of community‑rooted, linguistically inclusive care.
60b5aeedc1b6: 1. Why care is so hard to reach
f8b1a0632da1: <t1>Distance.</t1> About 80% of Guatemala’s physicians work in Guatemala City, leaving rural areas chronically underserved. In Alta Verapaz, where many Indigenous communities live, 23% of the population is more than an hour from any basic health facility. Rural Indigenous families often travel 3–6 hours to reach a diagnostic facility, and transport can cost Q100–Q150, often more than a family’s weekly income.
68f40678ee06: <t1>Cost.</t1> Private clinics charge about Q300 ($40) per visit, while rural families often earn Q15–Q25 a day. A single visit can cost the equivalent of several days of income.
eacffa2a05aa: <t1>Language.</t1> Guatemala has 25 Indigenous languages and 40% of the population identifies as Indigenous, yet most healthcare providers speak only Spanish. For K’iche’‑speaking patients, miscommunication leads to misdiagnosis, mistrust and avoidance of care.
b3ee2ff382e0: <t1>Underfunding.</t1> Guatemala’s total health spending is about $392 per person per year (WHO, 2023), a fraction of what wealthier countries spend. The system is divided into public, private and social security sectors, and the public sector carries most rural care while being the most under‑resourced. Rural clinics often lack medications, imaging, labs, electronic records and trained personnel, and maternal and child health indicators remain among the most challenging in Central America.
6744b637e4c1: Together, distance, cost, language and underfunding create preventable suffering.
3632b900bd35: Bringing clinicians and diagnostics closer to home removes the hours‑long trips many highland families face.
718536699faa: Aldea Pitzal represents the lived reality behind national statistics. Against this backdrop, Dr. Pelico provides affordable, linguistically accessible and continuous care.

958ce46ecb2f: <t1>Ethical, affordable care:</t1> Q25 ($3) per visit, compared with Q300 ($40) at private clinics.
ae91b7164965: <t1>Ultrasound on site</t1> for early pregnancy monitoring, high‑risk maternal conditions, abdominal and pelvic diagnostics, and chronic disease monitoring.
dbd6e16a401b: <t1>A K’iche’‑language EMR</t1> that supports ethical data tracking, continuity of care, research readiness and community‑level insights.
3afbfc18e5c5: 3. Measuring change: the Community Impact Measure (CIM)
ebffee86e986: PAMA’s Equity in Action program measures impact with the Community Impact Measure, which scores four domains from 0 to 5 each, for a total of 0 to 20:
6cd4988ed3f0: <t1>Access to Care</t1> — clinic visits, reduced travel burden, affordability, night‑time urgent care
6d95c58f0ad8: <t1>Clinical Empowerment</t1> — diagnostic capacity, ultrasound training, EMR‑supported decision‑making
f8950cf5475f: <t1>Community Trust</t1> — follow‑up rates, retention, participation, trilingual communication
cf9bdebb744b: <t1>Infrastructure Sustainability</t1> — staffing, digital systems, continuity‑of‑care protocols, research readiness
f9f4aba9314c: Early stage: limited diagnostics, minimal staffing, high referral burden
aaabf8d781d0: Strong impact: ultrasound and expanded hours improve affordability and retention
3105f028b368: Transformational: ultrasound training completed and new nurses hired
1897df23adbf: 60% fewer unnecessary referrals to Guatemala City
a7c72d85b531: 2026: new nurses, expanded service hours, stronger follow‑up systems

3e1277d82c3b: The combination of technology, language access, affordability and 24‑hour availability has produced a structural change in community health. By 2026 the clinic reached a CIM score of 17, reflecting sustained access, high diagnostic autonomy, strong community trust and durable infrastructure. This trajectory shows that Indigenous‑led, community‑rooted, digitally supported care can rapidly and measurably reduce health disparities in rural Guatemala.
95352f710c93: Guatemala’s public health sector doesn’t just need more funding; it needs structural transformation that begins with trust, language access and local leadership. Together with our partners, PAMA envisions a network of Indigenous‑led clinics across Guatemala, each with solar‑powered diagnostic tools, culturally adapted health records and staff fluent in local languages, and a model that can scale to other underserved regions.
b18c7067bf07: These efforts are not charity. They are investments in hemispheric health equity, rooted in the belief that local providers must lead the transformation of their own systems.

fcc2143f5a42: Dr. Renee Quarterman founded P4C on a simple belief: healthcare is a hemispheric responsibility, not a national one. Through organizing, community education and coalition‑building, she has created a space where physicians, students and neighbors learn about Cuba’s medical model and contribute to humanitarian support.
acf94e70d26e: In 2026, PAMA became P4C’s fiscal sponsor, giving the group nonprofit infrastructure, financial transparency systems and logistics support, so Dr. Quarterman can focus on the mission instead of paperwork.

1fabe6556d41: Sara Gómez (1942–1974) was the first woman to direct a feature film in Cuba. Her documentaries and her one feature show everyday Cuban life, with frank looks at race, gender, family and work.
